title: Orbital Floor Fractures: Clinical Mastery & Surgical Management
summary: A comprehensive guide to the diagnosis, management, and surgical repair of orbital floor 'blowout' fractures. Master the assessment of ocular motility, infraorbital nerve integrity, and surgical thresholds based on the latest Kanski-level evidence.

sections.title: Definition & Anatomy
sections.content: An orbital floor fracture, often termed a 'blowout fracture', occurs from blunt trauma to the orbit. The sudden increase in intraorbital pressure is transmitted to the weakest part of the bony orbit: the thin maxillary bone medial to the infraorbital groove. This often results in herniation of orbital fat and sometimes the inferior rectus muscle into the maxillary sinus.

sections.title: Red Flags: Emergency Signs
content: Oculocardiac Reflex: Bradycardia/nausea during manipulation (pediatric emergency!)
Traumatic Optic Neuropathy (Afferent Pupillary Defect)
Open Globe Injury (must be ruled out first)
Infraorbital nerve anesthesia (suggests significant nerve impingement)
Globe rupture or retrobulbar hemorrhage

sections.title: Clinical Features
content: Periorbital ecchymosis and edema
Enophthalmos (often masked by swelling initially)
Diplopia, specifically in vertical gaze
Infraorbital nerve paresthesia (cheek/upper lip)
Restriction of globe motility (forced duction test positive)

branches: Pure Blowout: Orbital rim remains intact

rows: Acute tension, proptosis, loss of vision
Fever, elevated WBC, pain on movement

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Visual acuity, pupils, and slit-lamp exam (rule out globe rupture).
Step 2: Hertel exophthalmometry to measure enophthalmos.
Step 3: Forced duction test to differentiate restriction vs. muscle weakness.
Step 4: Non-contrast CT Orbit (Axial/Coronal) - Coronal view is gold standard.

sections.title: Management Protocol
content: Conservative: Oral antibiotics (Augmentin), nasal decongestants, avoid nose blowing.
Surgical Threshold: Diplopia within 30 degrees of primary gaze.
Surgical Threshold: Enophthalmos > 2mm.
Surgical Threshold: Large fractures (>50% floor surface area).
Timing: Urgent for pediatric trapdoor (within 24-48hrs), elective for others (1-2 weeks).

sections.title: Surgical Techniques
content: Approach: Subciliary, transconjunctival (preseptal or retroseptal), or transcaruncular.
Release: Careful dissection of herniated contents back into the orbit.
Reconstruction: Use of porous polyethylene, titanium mesh, or absorbable implants.
Assessment: Post-placement forced duction test must be negative before closure.

content.explanation: D: Diplopia (persistent), E: Enophthalmos (>2mm), E: Eye muscle restriction (positive forced duction), P: Piece of bone/fat (large defect/Trapdoor).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always check the globe: 10-15% of blowout fractures have associated ocular injury.
Pediatric trapdoor fractures often show no external signs (white-eyed).
Avoid late surgery if possible: scarring leads to poor motility recovery.
The infraorbital nerve runs in the floor; numbness is a classic finding.
